opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
The detail about “seven demons” (from Gospel of Luke 8:2 and echoed in Gospel of Mark 16:9) is not there to be overlooked.  It is precise in its placement.  The number “seven” is not random–it means totality.  In scripture, it means completeness/fullness.  So when it says Mary Magdalene had “seven demons,” it is not just counting and saying, Wow, it is saying she was completely bound, her condition was total, not partial, there was nothing in her that wasn’t touched by brokenness.  We are able to see her before and after. If this detail were removed, then Mary would become just “a follower”.  But with the detail, she becomes a living testimony of total restoration, someone who went from complete bondage to complete freedom.  

That is why she is the first witness of the resurrection.
She is of them the most radically freed and is the first to see Him risen.  Then you have the apostles who walked with him for years, and she comes running back……yet they do not believe.  Mary was broken and fully restored, fully transformed, could see, but the apostles could not.  Although the proximity to Jesus was still there.  We expect the apostles to show immediate belief, and Mary, perhaps through her history of brokenness as being uncertain, emotional, and maybe even unreliable.  

Instead, it flips.  Mary sees clearly, the faithful witness, the Apostles are skeptical and resistant. Mary receives everything, a complete transformation, so she recognizes him immediately, no internal resistance, no filtering, no control.  The Apostles are still trying to process, still having control, still wanting understanding, that they miss what is in front of them. They have hardness of hearts.  Jesus rebukes them for their resistance to what God is doing, even when trusted witnesses tell them.  
This emphasizes how God works.  He spreads through those who have truly received, not just observed. 
The apostles had proximity. She had a transformation. And it was the one fully healed who first proclaimed the Resurrection.
Now the call is not to strive to reach Him—but to see Him as He is, without resistance, without control, without rewriting His work into our expectations.

But this does not require a complete transformation first.  Mary Magdalene did not make herself whole—Christ did. What set her apart was not perfection, but that she did not resist what had been done in her.

Most of us are not there. We still hold on, still filter, still try to understand before we receive. But clarity does not come at the end of transformation—it begins the moment we stop resisting it.

Even while healing, we are still being invited to recognize Him. Not perfectly.

But truly.
